blocks.en: Unit 6 · Exodus — Redemption and Deliverance
blocks.es_reference: Unidad 6 · Éxodo — Redención y Liberación

blocks.en: 1. Introduction to Exodus: The Birth of a Nation
blocks.es_reference: 1. Introducción a Éxodo: El Nacimiento de una Nación

blocks.en: The book of Exodus is the connecting link between God's promise to Abraham and the beginning of the theocratic kingdom of Israel under Moses. Conservative scholarship holds to Mosaic authorship, dating the book to the late 13th century BC (around 1290, though some date it earlier to about 1450 BC). Jesus Himself affirmed that Moses wrote Exodus (Mark 7:10). The central events are the miraculous deliverance of Israel from slavery in Egypt and the establishment of the Mosaic covenant as the constitution of the new nation. The first 18 chapters portray God as Savior and Provider. The second section reveals God's character through detailed laws. The conclusion gives instructions for the tabernacle, which foreshadows Christ. Genesis ended in a coffin with a promise; Exodus begins with that promise being kept.
blocks.es_reference: El libro de Éxodo es el eslabón de conexión entre la promesa de Dios a Abraham y el comienzo del reino teocrático de Israel bajo Moisés. La erudición conservadora sostiene la autoría mosaica, datando el libro a finales del siglo XIII a.C. (alrededor de 1290, aunque algunos lo datan antes, hacia 1450 a.C.). Jesús mismo afirmó que Moisés escribió Éxodo (Marcos 7:10). Los eventos centrales son la liberación milagrosa de Israel de la esclavitud en Egipto y el establecimiento del pacto mosaico como la constitución de la nueva nación. Los primeros 18 capítulos presentan a Dios como Salvador y Proveedor. La segunda sección revela el carácter de Dios a través de leyes detalladas. La conclusión da instrucciones para el tabernáculo, que presagia a Cristo. Génesis terminó en un ataúd con una promesa; Éxodo comienza con esa promesa siendo cumplida.

blocks.en: Exodus 1:7 (NKJV): "But the children of Israel were fruitful and increased abundantly, multiplied and grew exceedingly mighty; and the land was filled with them."
blocks.es_reference: Éxodo 1:7 (RVG): "Y los hijos de Israel fructificaron y se multiplicaron, y fueron aumentados y fortalecidos en gran manera, y la tierra se llenó de ellos."

blocks.en: 2. A New Pharaoh Who Knew Not Joseph
blocks.es_reference: 2. Un Nuevo Faraón Que No Conocía a José

blocks.en: A new king arose in Egypt who had no appreciation for Joseph's character or achievements. He saw the rapidly multiplying Israelites as a threat. "Look," he said, "the people of the children of Israel are more and mightier than we." His solution was ruthless oppression: slave masters, forced labor, and the construction of the store cities Pithom and Rameses. But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied. God was sovereignly blessing His people even under persecution. When the oppression didn't work, Pharaoh ordered the Hebrew midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, to kill all male babies at birth. The midwives feared God and disobeyed, letting the boys live. When confronted, they explained that Hebrew women were vigorous and gave birth before the midwives arrived. God was kind to the midwives and gave them families of their own. Finally, Pharaoh commanded all his people: "Every son who is born you shall cast into the river."
blocks.es_reference: Surgió un nuevo rey en Egipto que no apreciaba el carácter ni los logros de José. Vio a los israelitas multiplicándose rápidamente como una amenaza. "Mira", dijo, "el pueblo de los hijos de Israel es más y más fuerte que nosotros". Su solución fue una opresión despiadada: amos de esclavos, trabajo forzado y la construcción de las ciudades almacén Pitón y Ramesés. Pero cuanto más los oprimían, más se multiplicaban. Dios estaba bendiciendo soberanamente a Su pueblo incluso bajo persecución. Cuando la opresión no funcionó, Faraón ordenó a las parteras hebreas, Sifrá y Puá, que mataran a todos los niños varones al nacer. Las parteras temieron a Dios y desobedecieron, dejando vivir a los niños. Cuando fueron confrontadas, explicaron que las mujeres hebreas eran vigorosas y daban a luz antes de que llegaran las parteras. Dios fue bondadoso con las parteras y les dio familias. Finalmente, Faraón ordenó a todo su pueblo: "Echad al río a todo hijo que nazca".

blocks.en: 3. The Birth and Preservation of Moses
blocks.es_reference: 3. El Nacimiento y Preservación de Moisés

blocks.en: A man from the house of Levi married a Levite woman. She gave birth to a son and hid him for three months. When she could no longer hide him, she made a papyrus basket, covered it with tar and pitch, and placed the child among the reeds by the Nile. The child's sister stood at a distance to see what would happen. Pharaoh's daughter came down to bathe, saw the basket, and sent her maid to get it. When she opened it, she saw the crying baby and had compassion. The sister suggested finding a Hebrew nurse — who turned out to be the baby's own mother. Pharaoh's daughter paid Moses' mother to nurse her own son. When the child grew, she brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, who named him Moses, saying, "Because I drew him out of the water." In God's mercy, Moses' parents not only got their son back but were paid to care for him — and the enemy's house funded the deliverer's preparation.
blocks.es_reference: Un hombre de la casa de Leví se casó con una mujer levita. Ella dio a luz un hijo y lo escondió durante tres meses. Cuando ya no pudo esconderlo, hizo una canasta de papiro, la cubrió con asfalto y brea, y colocó al niño entre los juncos del Nilo. La hermana del niño se quedó a distancia para ver qué sucedería. La hija de Faraón bajó a bañarse, vio la canasta y envió a su criada a buscarla. Cuando la abrió, vio al bebé llorando y tuvo compasión. La hermana sugirió buscar una nodriza hebrea — que resultó ser la propia madre del bebé. La hija de Faraón pagó a la madre de Moisés para que criara a su propio hijo. Cuando el niño creció, lo llevó a la hija de Faraón, quien lo llamó Moisés, diciendo: "Porque de las aguas lo saqué". Por la misericordia de Dios, los padres de Moisés no solo recuperaron a su hijo sino que les pagaron para cuidarlo — y la casa del enemigo financió la preparación del libertador.

blocks.en: Pastoral Note: God's providence often works through the most unlikely circumstances. A baby in a basket becomes the deliverer of a nation. The Egyptian princess who saved Moses funded his Hebrew education for years. No situation is too desperate for God to redeem.
blocks.es_reference: Nota Pastoral: La providencia de Dios a menudo obra a través de las circunstancias más improbables. Un bebé en una canasta se convierte en el libertador de una nación. La princesa egipcia que salvó a Moisés financió su educación hebrea durante años. No hay situación demasiado desesperada para que Dios la redima.

blocks.en: 4. Moses: From Prince to Shepherd to Deliverer
blocks.es_reference: 4. Moisés: De Príncipe a Pastor a Libertador

blocks.en: Moses grew up in Pharaoh's house, educated in all the wisdom of Egypt. But at age forty, he saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his own people. Looking this way and that, and seeing no one, he killed the Egyptian and hid him in the sand. The next day, he tried to stop two Hebrews from fighting, and one said, "Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? Do you intend to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?" Moses realized his act was known. Pharaoh sought to kill him, and Moses fled to Midian. There he defended seven daughters of the priest of Midian at a well, married one (Zipporah), and became a shepherd. For forty years, Moses learned humility and patience in the wilderness — far from the palace, far from his dreams of delivering Israel. God spent forty years emptying him out so He could fill him. The man at eighty was not the man at forty. Self-confidence had given way to God-dependence.
blocks.es_reference: Moisés creció en la casa de Faraón, educado en toda la sabiduría de Egipto. Pero a los cuarenta años, vio a un egipcio golpeando a un hebreo, uno de los suyos. Mirando a un lado y a otro, y al no ver a nadie, mató al egipcio y lo escondió en la arena. Al día siguiente, trató de detener a dos hebreos que peleaban, y uno dijo: "¿Quién te ha puesto a ti como príncipe y juez sobre nosotros? ¿Piensas matarme como mataste al egipcio?" Moisés se dio cuenta de que su acto se conocía. Faraón buscó matarlo, y Moisés huyó a Madián. Allí defendió a siete hijas del sacerdote de Madián en un pozo, se casó con una (Séfora) y se convirtió en pastor. Durante cuarenta años, Moisés aprendió humildad y paciencia en el desierto — lejos del palacio, lejos de sus sueños de liberar a Israel. Dios pasó cuarenta años vaciándolo para poder llenarlo. El hombre a los ochenta no era el hombre a los cuarenta. La autoconfianza había dado paso a la dependencia de Dios.

blocks.en: 5. The Burning Bush: Holy Ground
blocks.es_reference: 5. La Zarza Ardiente: Tierra Santa

blocks.en: Moses was pastoring the flock of his father-in-law Jethro when he came to Horeb, the mountain of God. The angel of the Lord appeared in a flame of fire from the midst of a bush. The bush burned but was not consumed. Moses turned aside to see this great sight. God called to him from the bush: "Moses, Moses!" He said, "Here I am." Then God said, "Do not draw near this place. Take your sandals off your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground." The command to remove sandals meant: don't let anything separate you from Me. Then God declared: "I am the God of your father — the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." Moses hid his face, afraid to look upon God. The bush that burned without being consumed is itself a picture of Israel in Egypt — afflicted but not destroyed, suffering but not extinguished.
blocks.es_reference: Moisés pastoreaba el rebaño de su suegro Jetro cuando llegó a Horeb, el monte de Dios. El ángel de Jehová se le apareció en una llama de fuego en medio de una zarza. La zarza ardía pero no se consumía. Moisés se apartó para ver esta gran visión. Dios lo llamó desde la zarza: "¡Moisés, Moisés!" Él respondió: "Heme aquí". Entonces Dios dijo: "No te acerques; quita tus sandalias de tus pies, porque el lugar donde estás es tierra santa". La orden de quitar las sandalias significaba: no dejes que nada te separe de Mí. Luego Dios declaró: "Yo soy el Dios de tu padre, Dios de Abraham, Dios de Isaac y Dios de Jacob". Moisés escondió su rostro, temiendo mirar a Dios. La zarza que ardía sin consumirse es en sí una imagen de Israel en Egipto — afligido pero no destruido, sufriendo pero no extinguido.

blocks.en: Exodus 3:7-8 (NKJV): "And the Lord said: 'I have surely seen the oppression of My people who are in Egypt, and have heard their cry because of their taskmasters, for I know their sorrows. So I have come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians, and to bring them up from that land to a good and large land, to a land flowing with milk and honey.'"
blocks.es_reference: Éxodo 3:7-8 (RVG): "Y dijo Jehová: Bien he visto la aflicción de mi pueblo que está en Egipto, y he oído su clamor a causa de sus exactores; porque he conocido sus angustias. Y he descendido para librarlos de mano de los egipcios, y sacarlos de aquella tierra a una tierra buena y ancha, a tierra que fluye leche y miel."

blocks.en: 6. The Call of Moses: "Who Am I?"
blocks.es_reference: 6. El Llamado de Moisés: "¿Quién Soy Yo?"

blocks.en: God commissioned Moses: "Come now, I will send you to Pharaoh, that you may bring My people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt." Moses responded, "Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh?" God's answer was not what Moses expected. He did not list Moses' qualifications. He said, "I will certainly be with you." The power of the calling depends not on the one called, but on the One who calls. Moses then asked for God's name. God replied, "I AM WHO I AM" (Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh). This name, YHWH (Yahweh), speaks to God's self-existence and eternal presence. He depends on nothing. He never changes. He will be whatever His people need Him to be at the moment they need it. God instructed Moses to gather the elders of Israel and go to Pharaoh, asking for a three-day journey into the wilderness to sacrifice to the Lord. God also revealed that Pharaoh would not let them go except under compulsion, so God would stretch out His hand and strike Egypt with wonders.
blocks.es_reference: Dios comisionó a Moisés: "Ven, pues, ahora, y te enviaré a Faraón, para que saques a mi pueblo, los hijos de Israel, de Egipto". Moisés respondió: "¿Quién soy yo para que vaya a Faraón?" La respuesta de Dios no fue la que Moisés esperaba. No enumeró las cualificaciones de Moisés. Dijo: "Ciertamente yo estaré contigo". El poder del llamado depende no del llamado, sino del que llama. Luego Moisés preguntó por el nombre de Dios. Dios respondió: "YO SOY EL QUE SOY" (Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh). Este nombre, YHWH (Yahvéh), habla de la autoexistencia y presencia eterna de Dios. Él no depende de nada. Nunca cambia. Será lo que Su pueblo necesite en el momento que lo necesite. Dios instruyó a Moisés a reunir a los ancianos de Israel e ir a Faraón, pidiendo un viaje de tres días al desierto para sacrificar a Jehová. Dios también reveló que Faraón no los dejaría ir excepto bajo compulsión, así que Dios extendería Su mano y heriría a Egipto con maravillas.

blocks.en: 7. Moses' Excuses and God's Answers
blocks.es_reference: 7. Las Excusas de Moisés y las Respuestas de Dios

blocks.en: Moses gave five objections. First: "They won't believe me." God gave three signs: staff turning to serpent and back; hand becoming leprous and restored; water from the Nile turning to blood. Second: "I am not eloquent." God reminded him that He made the mouth. Third: "Send someone else." God became angry but appointed Aaron as his spokesman. Fourth: "I don't know Your name." God revealed YHWH. Fifth: "The people won't listen." God had already promised they would. After forty years of humility training, Moses still struggled to trust his own calling. The lesson: God doesn't call the qualified; He qualifies the called. Every great servant of God in Scripture protested first and was sent anyway. The right response to a divine call is "Here I am" — not "Here is what I cannot do."
blocks.es_reference: Moisés dio cinco objeciones. Primero: "No me creerán". Dios dio tres señales: vara convertida en serpiente y viceversa; mano leprosa y restaurada; agua del Nilo convertida en sangre. Segundo: "No soy elocuente". Dios le recordó que Él hizo la boca. Tercero: "Envía a otro". Dios se enojó pero nombró a Aarón como su portavoz. Cuarto: "No conozco Tu nombre". Dios reveló YHWH. Quinto: "El pueblo no escuchará". Dios ya había prometido que sí. Después de cuarenta años de entrenamiento en humildad, Moisés aún luchaba por confiar en su propio llamado. La lección: Dios no llama a los calificados; califica a los llamados. Todo gran siervo de Dios en la Escritura protestó primero y fue enviado de todos modos. La respuesta correcta a un llamado divino es "Heme aquí" — no "Esto es lo que no puedo hacer".

blocks.en: Application for Pastors: How many times have you said, "I can't do this"? God's answer is always: "I will be with you." Your inadequacy is not a problem; it is the prerequisite for His power to be seen.
blocks.es_reference: Aplicación para Pastores: ¿Cuántas veces has dicho: "No puedo hacer esto"? La respuesta de Dios es siempre: "Yo estaré contigo". Tu insuficiencia no es un problema; es el requisito previo para que Su poder sea visto.

blocks.en: 8. The Plagues: Mocking the Gods of Egypt
blocks.es_reference: 8. Las Plagas: Burlándose de los Dioses de Egipto

blocks.en: Moses and Aaron confronted Pharaoh, demanding, "Let My people go." Pharaoh refused. God then sent ten plagues, each one an attack on specific Egyptian deities. They fell in three cycles of three, with the tenth as the climax. The first cycle: Water turned to blood (mocking Hapi, the Nile god, and Isis, goddess of the Nile); Frogs (mocking Hequet, the frog-headed goddess of birth); Gnats (mocking Set, god of the desert). The second cycle: Flies (mocking Re, the sun god); Death of livestock (mocking Hathor the cow-headed goddess and Apis the bull god); Boils (mocking Sekhmet, goddess of disease, and Isis, goddess of healing). The third cycle: Hail (mocking Nut the sky goddess and Osiris the crop god); Locusts (mocking Nut and Osiris again); Darkness (mocking Re and Horus, the sun gods). The tenth plague — death of the firstborn — mocked Min (god of reproduction), Hequet, and Isis. By the end, every god of Egypt had been shown to be impotent. The Lord alone is God.
blocks.es_reference: Moisés y Aarón confrontaron a Faraón, exigiendo: "Deja ir a mi pueblo". Faraón se negó. Dios entonces envió diez plagas, cada una un ataque a deidades egipcias específicas. Cayeron en tres ciclos de tres, con la décima como clímax. El primer ciclo: Agua convertida en sangre (burlándose de Hapi, el dios del Nilo, e Isis, diosa del Nilo); Ranas (burlándose de Hequet, la diosa del parto con cabeza de rana); Piojos (burlándose de Set, dios del desierto). El segundo ciclo: Moscas (burlándose de Ra, el dios sol); Muerte del ganado (burlándose de Hathor, la diosa con cabeza de vaca, y Apis, el dios toro); Úlceras (burlándose de Sekhmet, diosa de las enfermedades, e Isis, diosa de la curación). El tercer ciclo: Granizo (burlándose de Nut, la diosa del cielo, y Osiris, dios de los cultivos); Langostas (burlándose de Nut y Osiris nuevamente); Tinieblas (burlándose de Ra y Horus, los dioses del sol). La décima plaga — muerte de los primogénitos — se burló de Min (dios de la reproducción), Hequet e Isis. Al final, todos los dioses de Egipto habían mostrado ser impotentes. Solo Jehová es Dios.

blocks.en: 9. The Passover: A Memorial of Redemption
blocks.es_reference: 9. La Pascua: Un Memorial de Redención

blocks.en: Before the tenth plague, God gave instructions for the Passover. Each household was to take a lamb without blemish on the tenth day of the month. On the fourteenth day at twilight, they were to kill the lamb and put its blood on the two doorposts and the lintel of their houses. They were to eat the lamb roasted with fire, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, with their loins girded, sandals on their feet, and staff in hand — in haste. That night, the Lord passed through Egypt and struck all the firstborn, from the firstborn of Pharaoh to the firstborn of the captive. But when He saw the blood on the doorposts, He passed over those houses. The blood was the sign. Not their goodness, not their heritage — only the blood. This was the first gospel: the innocent substitute dies, the guilty go free.
blocks.es_reference: Antes de la décima plaga, Dios dio instrucciones para la Pascua. Cada familia debía tomar un cordero sin defecto el décimo día del mes. El día catorce al atardecer, debían matar el cordero y poner su sangre en los dos postes y el dintel de sus casas. Debían comer el cordero asado al fuego, con pan sin levadura y hierbas amargas, con sus lomos ceñidos, sandalias en sus pies y bastón en la mano — apresuradamente. Esa noche, Jehová pasó por Egipto e hirió a todos los primogénitos, desde el primogénito de Faraón hasta el primogénito del cautivo. Pero cuando vio la sangre en los postes, pasó por alto esas casas. La sangre era la señal. No su bondad, no su herencia — solo la sangre. Este fue el primer evangelio: el sustituto inocente muere, el culpable queda libre.

blocks.en: Exodus 12:13 (NKJV): "Now the blood shall be a sign for you on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you; and the plague shall not be on you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt."
blocks.es_reference: Éxodo 12:13 (RVG): "Y la sangre os será por señal en las casas donde vosotros estéis; y veré la sangre y pasaré de vosotros, y no habrá en vosotros plaga de mortandad cuando hiera la tierra de Egipto."

blocks.en: 10. The Exodus: Plundering Egypt
blocks.es_reference: 10. El Éxodo: Despojando a Egipto

blocks.en: At midnight, the Lord struck all the firstborn of Egypt. There was a great cry, for there was no house where there was not someone dead. Pharaoh called for Moses and Aaron and said, "Rise, go out from among my people, you and the children of Israel." The Egyptians urged the people to go quickly, saying, "We shall all be dead." The Israelites asked their neighbors for articles of silver and gold and clothing, and the Lord gave them favor. They plundered Egypt — not as theft, but as back wages for 400 years of slavery. The gold and silver would later be used to build the tabernacle. About 600,000 men, plus women and children, left Egypt that night — a logistical miracle. And they left in such haste that their dough had no time to leaven. The Exodus had begun. The Passover lamb points directly to Jesus, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (John 1:29). His blood, applied by faith, causes the judgment to pass over us. As Paul wrote, "Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed for us" (1 Corinthians 5:7).
blocks.es_reference: A medianoche, Jehová hirió a todos los primogénitos de Egipto. Hubo un gran clamor, porque no había casa donde no hubiera un muerto. Faraón llamó a Moisés y a Aarón y dijo: "Levantaos, salid de en medio de mi pueblo, vosotros y los hijos de Israel". Los egipcios urgieron al pueblo a irse rápidamente, diciendo: "Todos moriremos". Los israelitas pidieron a sus vecinos objetos de plata y oro y vestidos, y Jehová les dio favor. Despojaron a Egipto — no como robo, sino como salario atrasado por 400 años de esclavitud. El oro y la plata serían usados más tarde para construir el tabernáculo. Aproximadamente 600,000 hombres, más mujeres y niños, salieron de Egipto esa noche — un milagro logístico. Y salieron tan apresuradamente que su masa no tuvo tiempo de leudarse. El Éxodo había comenzado. El cordero pascual apunta directamente a Jesús, el Cordero de Dios que quita el pecado del mundo (Juan 1:29). Su sangre, aplicada por fe, hace que el juicio pase sobre nosotros. Como Pablo escribió: "Cristo, nuestra pascua, fue sacrificado por nosotros" (1 Corintios 5:7).

blocks.en: The Route of the Exodus
blocks.es_reference: La Ruta del Éxodo

blocks.en: A traditional reconstruction of Israel’s journey out of Egypt — from Rameses and Succoth, through the wilderness to Mount Sinai (Horeb), and on toward Canaan by way of Kadesh-barnea. The exact route, the place of the sea crossing, and the location of Mount Sinai are all debated among scholars; this map presents one traditional view.
blocks.es_reference: Una reconstrucción tradicional del viaje de Israel desde Egipto — desde Ramesés y Sucot, a través del desierto hasta el Monte Sinaí (Horeb), y hacia Canaán por Cades-barnea. La ruta exacta, el lugar del cruce del mar y la ubicación del Monte Sinaí son debatidos entre los eruditos; este mapa presenta una visión tradicional. (El diagrama está en inglés.)

Πεντάτευχος

mc.stem: Who did Jesus affirm as the author of Exodus?
mc.why: Correct! Jesus quoted Exodus as written by Moses in Mark 7:10.

mc.stem: What was the name of the store cities the Israelites built for Pharaoh?
mc.why: Yes. Pithom and Rameses were store cities built with forced Hebrew labor.

mc.stem: What were the names of the Hebrew midwives who feared God and disobeyed Pharaoh?
mc.why: Correct. Shiphrah and Puah are honored for fearing God more than Pharaoh.

mc.stem: What does the name 'Moses' mean?
mc.why: Yes. Pharaoh's daughter said, 'Because I drew him out of the water.'

mc.stem: How long did Moses live in Midian as a shepherd before God called him?
mc.why: Correct. Moses was 40 when he fled Egypt and 80 when he returned — 40 years in Midian.

mc.stem: What did God tell Moses to remove before approaching the burning bush?
mc.why: Yes. 'Take your sandals off your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground.'

mc.stem: What does the name 'I AM' (YHWH) signify about God?
options: God is only a God of the past
mc.why: Correct. 'Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh' — 'I will be who I will be' — speaks to God's self-existence.

mc.stem: What was Moses' first objection when God called him?
options: 'Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh?'
mc.why: Yes. Moses asked, 'Who am I?' — focusing on his own inadequacy rather than God's power.

mc.stem: Which plague turned the Nile River into blood?
mc.why: Correct. The first plague was water turned to blood, mocking Hapi, the Nile god.

mc.stem: Which Egyptian goddess with a frog's head was mocked by the second plague?
mc.why: Yes. Hequet, the frog-headed goddess of birth, was powerless against the Lord.

mc.stem: What was the ninth plague?
mc.why: Correct. Darkness for three days — mocking Ra and Horus, the sun gods.

mc.stem: Each plague was designed to do what?
options: Mock the gods of Egypt and show the Lord alone is God
mc.why: Yes. Every plague was an attack on specific Egyptian deities, proving their impotence.

mc.stem: What was the final plague that broke Pharaoh's resistance?
mc.why: Correct. The death of every firstborn — from Pharaoh's son to the captive's son.

mc.stem: What did the Israelites put on their doorposts to be spared from the tenth plague?
options: The blood of the Passover lamb
mc.why: Yes. 'When I see the blood, I will pass over you.' Not their goodness — the blood alone.

mc.stem: The Passover lamb had to be without what?
mc.why: Correct. A male without blemish — foreshadowing Christ, the spotless Lamb.

mc.stem: How were the Israelites to eat the Passover meal?
options: With loins girded, sandals on, staff in hand — in haste
mc.why: Yes. They were ready to leave — dressed for a journey, eating in haste.

mc.stem: What did the Israelites ask from the Egyptians before they left?
options: Articles of silver, gold, and clothing
mc.why: Correct. They plundered Egypt — back wages for 400 years of slavery.

mc.stem: Approximately how many Israelite men (not counting women and children) left Egypt?
mc.why: Yes. About 600,000 men — a logistical miracle of organization and supply.

mc.stem: What did the gold and silver taken from Egypt later become?
mc.why: Correct. The plunder of Egypt was later used to build the sanctuary for God.

mc.stem: How does the New Testament describe Jesus in relation to the Passover?
options: 'Jesus is the light of the world'
mc.why: Yes! 1 Corinthians 5:7 — 'Christ, our Passover, was sacrificed for us.'

sa.prompt: Why did a 'new king who did not know Joseph' arise, and what did he do to oppress Israel?
sa.model: A new dynasty arose that didn't honor Joseph's legacy. Pharaoh enslaved Israel, ordered male babies killed, but God's blessing continued.

sa.prompt: How did God protect Moses as an infant, and what irony is present in the account?
sa.model: Moses was hidden in a basket, found by Pharaoh's daughter, and his own mother was paid to nurse him — God's enemy funded His deliverer.

sa.prompt: What did Moses learn during his 40 years as a shepherd in Midian?
sa.model: God transformed Moses from an impulsive prince into a humble shepherd, teaching him to lead God's people with patience and reliance on God.

sa.prompt: What is the significance of God telling Moses to remove his sandals at the burning bush?
sa.model: Sandals represented separation from the holy ground. Removing them meant coming to God with nothing between — total surrender.

sa.prompt: What does 'I AM WHO I AM' (YHWH) reveal about God's nature?
sa.model: God exists in Himself, depends on nothing, and is eternally present. He will be what He will be — faithful to His promises.

sa.prompt: List five objections Moses raised to God's call and how God answered each.
sa.model: 1. 'Who am I?' → 'I will be with you.' 2. 'They won't believe' → Signs. 3. 'Not eloquent' → 'I made your mouth.' 4. 'Send another' → Aaron. 5. 'Your name?' → YHWH.

sa.prompt: Explain how the plagues mocked specific Egyptian gods. Give three examples.
sa.model: Water to blood mocked Hapi (Nile god). Frogs mocked Hequet (frog-headed birth goddess). Darkness mocked Ra (sun god).

sa.prompt: What were the instructions for the first Passover, and what did the blood signify?
sa.model: Take a spotless lamb, kill it, put blood on doorposts. When God saw the blood, He passed over that house — salvation by substitute.

sa.prompt: Why did the Israelites ask for silver, gold, and clothing from the Egyptians? Was this theft?
sa.model: It was payment for 400 years of unpaid labor. God gave them favor, and they left with what was rightfully theirs — and later used for the tabernacle.

sa.prompt: How does the Passover lamb point forward to Jesus Christ?
sa.model: Jesus is the spotless Lamb whose blood, applied by faith, causes God's judgment to pass over us. Paul explicitly calls Christ 'our Passover lamb.'
